one_liner: SOSP'23 three-FIFO-queue eviction policy: lower miss ratios than LRU, and over 6x CacheLib LRU's throughput at 16 threads.
what_it_does: S3-FIFO is a cache eviction algorithm, not a packaged cache. Its reference code is one eviction module (S3FIFO.c, about 520 lines of C) in the libCacheSim simulator. There you select it by name (`cachesim trace type s3fifo 1gb`) or through `S3FIFO_init(params, "small-size-ratio=0.10,ghost-size-ratio=0.90,move-to-main-threshold=2")`, which returns a `cache_t` with get/find/insert/evict/remove callbacks that replay a trace of object ids and sizes; it stores no values. For a real cache you port the policy: the authors' throughput prototype is a memory-management container (MMS3FIFO) in a 2023 CacheLib fork, and third-party libraries such as quick_cache (Rust) and Cloudflare's TinyUFO (S3-FIFO plus TinyLFU) implement variants.
how_it_is_fast: The algorithm rests on 'quick demotion'. Across 6594 production traces, a median 72% of objects in a window holding 10% of the trace's objects are one-hit wonders, so new objects go into a small FIFO S that takes 10% of the space. When an object reaches the tail of S, it moves to the main FIFO M if it was hit (threshold 2 in libCacheSim); otherwise it is evicted and its id goes into a ghost FIFO G, and a later miss that finds the id in G inserts straight into M. M works like CLOCK/FIFO-reinsertion with a 2-bit counter capped at 3. A cache hit only increments that counter atomically, so it moves no list node and takes no lock, whereas LRU promotion serializes on a lock. Insertion and eviction are queue-tail operations that can be done lock-free. The CacheLib prototype uses atomic doubly-linked lists and an atomic FIFO hash table for the ghost, which the paper says can hold 4-byte fingerprints.
when_to_use: Web, key-value and CDN object caches with skewed (Zipf-like) popularity and many one-hit wonders. At a cache size of 10% of the footprint, the paper finds S3-FIFO best by mean miss ratio on 10 of 14 datasets, and the author says it suits web workloads best.

Read-heavy, many-core in-memory caches where LRU's promote-on-hit lock is the bottleneck. A hit writes only a 2-bit counter, and the CacheLib prototype beat CacheLib's optimized LRU by more than 6x at 16 threads.

Flash caches that need an admission filter: keep S and the ghost in DRAM and write only objects hit twice to a FIFO flash tier. On the Wikimedia and Tencent Photo CDN traces this gave both fewer flash writes and a lower miss ratio than probabilistic admission or Flashield, even with DRAM at 0.1% of the cache size.
Replacing LRU in a slab-based cache when you want one static knob. Per the paper, miss ratios change little for most traces with S anywhere from 5% to 20% of the cache.
Evaluating candidate policies on your own traces first: libCacheSim runs s3fifo next to about 30 other policies (LRU, ARC, LIRS, W-TinyLFU, SIEVE...) in one command.
when_not_to_use: Database, search, analytics or old block workloads with loops or large scans. On the ARC DS1 and S3 traces, the author concedes that W-TinyLFU beats S3-FIFO. The Otter maintainer measured a 'quite serious' loss on DS1, and Caffeine's author calls its results across broader workloads 'great, good, bad, awful'.

Workloads where most objects are requested exactly twice, with the second request arriving after the object has left S. The paper names this as its adversarial pattern: the second request becomes a miss, which matters most for small caches (thousands of objects).

When you need a ready library from the authors. libCacheSim's version is simulation-only (ids and sizes, no values, glib dependency), and the CacheLib prototype is a research fork last pushed in December 2023. Upstream facebook/CacheLib ships no S3-FIFO container.

When multi-core speed is the main goal of a general-purpose library. Otter's author found that the paper's lock-free-queue design lost to BP-Wrapper caches (Ristretto, Theine) and rewrote Otter around BP-Wrapper. Otter v2.0.0 (June 2025) then replaced S3-FIFO with adaptive W-TinyLFU, and Caffeine's author reports close to 1B reads/s at 16 threads with a W-TinyLFU design.

Variable-size objects without slab classes: the paper's evaluation ignored object size. A ring-buffer implementation also wastes space under delete-heavy workloads, because deleted slots are not reused until eviction (paper, Sec. 4.2).

integration.form: source-drop (an algorithm; the reference C module is compiled into libCacheSim's CMake library and cachesim binary, and the CacheLib prototype is a templated MM container header inside a CacheLib fork)
integration.dependencies: libCacheSim: glib-2.0, argp, Threads, zstd (on by default for compressed traces), optional tcmalloc. CacheLib prototype: CacheLib's full stack, including folly (MPMCQueue, DistributedMutex).
integration.min_toolchain: libCacheSim: CMake 3.12+, a C compiler plus C++17 for its C++ parts, Ninja recommended, Release build by default. CacheLib prototype: CacheLib's contrib/build.sh toolchain, built RelWithDebInfo with Ninja; compiler not stated.
integration.platforms: libCacheSim CI runs on ubuntu-latest and macos-latest (clang); Windows not documented. The algorithm itself is portable C. The prototype's build.sh uses apt, so Debian/Ubuntu.
integration.thread_safety: libCacheSim: not documented. Each S3FIFO cache_t keeps per-call state in its struct (hit_on_ghost, req_local), so use one instance per thread; cachesim parallelizes by running separate caches. The CacheLib prototype records hits by setting a flag with no lock and links and unlinks nodes through atomic lists.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — in libCacheSim, 's3fifo' replaces 'lru' by name. In CacheLib, the prototype plugs in where MMLru goes (the MM container interface), but only in the 2023 fork. There is no drop-in LRU-cache library from the authors.

gotchas: Two versions exist. libCacheSim's 's3fifo' changed in October 2024 to insert new objects into M once S fills, before the first eviction. The SOSP'23 numbers come from the original, now 's3fifov0' (S3FIFOv0.c), so use that name to reproduce the paper.

Implementations differ from the paper. Algorithm 1 uses a 10% S, a 2-bit counter, promotion when freq > 1, and a ghost as large as M. libCacheSim sizes the ghost in bytes (0.9x cache size). The CacheLib prototype behind the 6x number uses a 5% S (pRatio_ = 0.05) and a single accessed bit, and sizes the ghost to half the object count at first eviction. Otter traced its hit-ratio jumps to ghost sizing.

libCacheSim will not cache an object whose size is at least the small queue's size (10% of cache bytes): insert returns NULL and can_insert returns false. Tiny caches or very large objects silently get no caching.

Evicting from M reinserts every tail object with a nonzero counter until it finds one at zero, so an eviction can walk a long run of recently hit objects (worst case O(n); counters capped at 3). Otter v1 advertised an O(1) worst case as a change from the paper's O(n).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick S3-FIFO over SIEVE (same repo, one queue) when the workload has scans or block-style access: its small queue plus ghost gives scan resistance, which the S3-FIFO paper says SIEVE lacks. Pick it over Caffeine or the W-TinyLFU C++ port when building a web/CDN/KV cache that needs lock-free hits and a single static knob, but keep adaptive W-TinyLFU for mixed database and analytics workloads, where S3-FIFO loses on loop-heavy traces such as DS1.
verified_claims_summary: Throughput was measured with the authors' S3-FIFO container in a 2023 CacheLib fork (linked lists for S and M, hash table for the ghost). It replayed a synthetic Zipf(1.0) trace of 100·n million requests over n million 4 KB objects in a closed loop, filling misses from pre-generated values. On CloudLab c6420 nodes (two 16-core Xeon Gold 6142 at 2.6 GHz per CloudLab's docs; turbo off, threads pinned, memory bound to one NUMA node) it exceeded 6x the throughput of CacheLib's optimized LRU at 16 threads, at LRU miss ratios of both 0.02 and 0.21. The build was RelWithDebInfo; the compiler is not named. Miss ratios come from libCacheSim simulation over 6594 traces, ignoring object size, against the lab's own reimplementations of the baselines (for example, W-TinyLFU without a doorkeeper or hill climbing). There S3-FIFO had the best mean on 10 of 14 datasets at a cache of 10% of the footprint and on 7 of 14 at 0.1%.
status_note: libCacheSim is actively maintained (Apache-2.0, 347 stars, pushed 2026-09-26), but it is a simulator, so production use means porting the roughly 500-line policy or adopting a third-party implementation such as quick_cache or TinyUFO. The CacheLib prototype fork has not been updated since December 2023 and never reached upstream, and s3fifo.com's adoption list still names Otter, which dropped S3-FIFO in v2.
